title: Preface
html:
Preface

Ask a group of engineers to design a new system and, before long, someone will walk to the whiteboard and start drawing boxes and arrows. They identify the components the application needs, such as an application programming interface (API), load balancer, database, cache, and queue. They then draw the connections to show how requests and data pass through the application.

The drawing is a useful start. Then someone should ask what happens when traffic doubles, when a dependency stops answering, or when two requests try to change the same record. Those questions can change the design more than the choice of framework or queue.

For instance, adding application instances may increase the number of requests processed concurrently. Each instance may also open its own database connections. If the database cannot support the combined work, customers can experience additional delay even though more application instances are available. Evaluating the change requires understanding which resource limits request completion and how the proposed change affects that resource.

Similar questions arise when introducing a cache, directing reads to a replica, or processing work asynchronously. What happens when frequently requested cache entries expire together? Which operations require a recent database value? How will an engineer establish whether work accepted by a queue produced the intended result?

The same concerns arise in new designs and changes to running services. A feature update may add a dependency, a configuration change may increase concurrency, and a retry may repeat an operation whose outcome the caller could not confirm. Before releasing a change, engineers need to assess its resource demand and the outcomes customers will receive when it fails.

This book examines those decisions through Baodium, a fictional commerce platform. Its application provides a continuing setting for exploring capacity, latency, state, caching, service communication, deployment, observability, asynchronous processing, and machine learning. The commerce examples give us concrete requests and records to investigate. The engineering questions apply wherever software shares finite resources, communicates across processes, and must recover from incomplete work.

Chapter 1 begins with Baodium adding personalized recommendations to its product pages. The new feature appears harmless during the first stage of rollout, but additional lookups eventually exhaust the available database connections. We follow what the engineers measured, why their initial release checks missed the warning signs, and which changes would have protected the existing traffic. Later chapters revisit earlier decisions as their effects become relevant elsewhere. Chapter 14 brings the accumulated experience into a design review for a regional launch. Appendix B then applies the same method to three classic design problems.

Following Baodium across the chapters lets us examine the consequences of earlier choices. Moving a task out of a synchronous request may shorten the customer’s wait, but the resulting queue requires backlog limits, duplicate handling, and a recovery procedure. We examine those later obligations alongside the response-time improvement that motivated the change.

Each chapter ends with a Hidden Assumptions review. It identifies a claim the design depends on, how that claim could fail, and the evidence available when the decision was made. It also names the measurement, the response if conditions change, and the person responsible for reviewing it.

The book assumes experience writing or maintaining an application that uses HTTP APIs and a database. Familiarity with basic SQL, transactions, and a deployment process will help. You do not need prior study of distributed systems. When an operation crosses from one process to another, we will examine what each process can know, which result it can guarantee, and what remains uncertain when the connection breaks.

Readers new to production engineering will benefit from following the chapters in order. Experienced engineers can use the worked examples and the hidden-assumptions review to examine an existing application. Engineers responsible for architecture reviews may find it useful to compare the regional launch in Chapter 14 with a proposal their own team is considering.

The examples use technologies such as PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, and Kubernetes. Their specific guarantees matter when implementing a design. The further-reading section provides sources for checking those guarantees against the versions and configurations in use.

Baodium is fictional, and its numerical examples should be read as illustrations of the reasoning under discussion. They are not performance benchmarks for the named technologies. Rates, durations, and thresholds apply to the stated conditions. Another application requires its own measurements.

The book focuses on how software services operate in production, including how they use resources, manage state, assign ownership, recover from interrupted work, and handle change. Security, privacy, compliance, and financial cost are covered in Appendix C as additional design constraints. The appendix provides a review you can apply to any proposal, but it is only a starting point and does not replace specialist review.

Three recurring features help you apply the ideas in practice.

Every chapter includes a Decide for yourself box. Each one presents a situation from the chapter, gives you the relevant numbers, and offers two to four reasonable actions. Stop at the box, choose an action, and write down your reasoning before reading the discussion that follows.

Some of these decisions can be settled with measurements or calculations. Others depend on trade-offs the business has to make. The discussion explains which evidence matters, what each option changes, and what you would give up by choosing one over another.

Several chapters include a short Public Postmortem, a summary of a publicly documented outage at a real company, so that you can set Baodium’s fictional incidents beside real ones and see the same mechanisms at work. Each box condenses the published account, so read the original before relying on a detail.

Appendix B then takes three familiar design problems: a URL shortener, a social timeline, and a notification service. Each includes capacity calculations, code, and failure drills.

AI tools can assist with calculations, code inspection, and the comparison of possible implementations. Engineers still need to establish which assumptions apply, which guarantees a proposal depends on, and what happens when its inputs are wrong. Throughout the book, we will practice making those judgments from the evidence available.

Adewale Obadimu
